1	# Assignment 2 — Learning a representation without labels
2	
3	**IDS 575: Machine Learning and Statistical Methods for Business Analytics · Fall 2026**
4	Released Wednesday, October 14 · **Due Thursday, November 5, 6:00 PM Central** · 10% of course grade
5	
6	Covers Lectures 6, 7 and 9: learned representations, training with early stopping, self-supervised pre-training, frozen representations, and fine-tuning.
7	
8	Expected effort: **4–6 focused hours**. The architectures, learning rates, sample sizes and splits are fixed for you below and implemented in `starter/kestrel.py`. You will not have to write a neural network or a training loop. Your work is to run one comparison, read it, and make a recommendation.
9	
10	Running the code needs only Lectures 6 and 7, which you have already had, so build the table in the first week. Lecture 9 on 22 October is what tells you how to read it, and Midterm 2 on 29 October covers the same material — so working through the table before the exam is good preparation for it. 12	---
13	
14	## The situation
15	
16	Kestrel Composites cures carbon-fibre panels for aircraft interiors. Every panel is cured in an instrumented autoclave that logs **160 process gauges**. Quality control is done by **destructive testing**: a panel is loaded to failure in a press and its interlaminar shear strength recorded.
17	
18	Destructive testing is expensive. Each test costs about **$1,400 in lab time and destroys a $3,000 panel**. Over five years the lab has tested **2,000 panels**. Meanwhile every panel ever cured — **20,000 of them** — has a complete gauge trace sitting in the historian, unlabelled and unused.
19	
20	Quality wants to predict strength from the gauges and test only the panels the model is unsure about. An engineer has fitted a regularized linear model on the 160 gauges. It is not accurate enough, and his read is that the fix is more data:
21	
22	> "We're at 2,000 tested panels. The model is still well short of what the spec needs. My recommendation is to budget another 2,000 tests over the next two years and re-fit."
23	
24	The Head of Quality wants a second opinion before signing off on **$8.8 million** of destroyed panels and lab time.
25	
26	## The three questions
27	
28	> 1. Will more destructive tests fix the current model?
29	> 2. Can the 20,000 unlabelled traces be made useful?
30	> 3. For the next panel family, how many destructive tests should Kestrel budget?
31	
32	You are not trying to win a modelling competition. There are no marks for beating the models prescribed below.
33	
34	---
35	
36	## What Handout 9 gives you
37	
38	Handout 9 establishes, with numbers, the results this assignment applies. You are not asked to rediscover them.
39	
40	- **§2** — self-supervised pre-training: hide part of an input, ask a network to rebuild it, and you have a training signal that needs no labels.
41	- **§2.1** — the three ways to use the resulting encoder: freeze it and fit something simple on top, fine-tune it, or ignore it and train from scratch.
42	- **§3.1–3.2** — pre-training substitutes for labelled data, so its value is greatest where labels are scarcest and shrinks as they accumulate. The rule by label regime: freeze at tens of labels, fine-tune at hundreds to thousands, train from scratch at tens of thousands.
43	- **§3.3** — the control that is usually omitted: an untrained encoder of identical shape. Without it you cannot separate "pre-training learned something" from "this architecture makes useful random features."
44	
45	Your job is to apply these to Kestrel's data and say what they imply for Kestrel's budget.
46	
47	---
48	
49	## The protocol
50	
51	Fixed, and implemented in `starter/kestrel.py`. You should not need to change any of it.
52	
53	| | Value |
54	|---|---|
55	| Label counts | *n* ∈ {50, 100, 250, 1000}, drawn from the 2,000 labelled panels |
56	| Label draws | **5 per cell**, from `label_subset(n, replicate)` |
57	| Pre-training seeds | **3** — pre-train three encoders, once each, and reuse them in every cell |
58	| Pre-training | Masked reconstruction: hide 30% of the gauges, rebuild them. 40 epochs, Adam at 3e-3 |
59	| Encoder | 160 → 64 → 16 → 160. The **representation is the first hidden layer**, 64 numbers |
60	| Frozen head | Ridge on those 64 numbers |
61	| Incumbent baseline | The same ridge, on the 160 raw gauges |
62	| From scratch | 160 → 64 → 1, Adam at 2e-3 |
63	| Fine-tuning | The same network started from the pre-trained encoder, Adam at 1e-3 |
64	| Early stopping | 25% inner validation split, patience 60, at most 800 epochs |
65	| Evaluation | `labeled_dev.csv` for everything in Part 1 |
66	
67	**Why five label draws and three pre-training seeds.** Both are sources of variation and both are large here. With 50 labels the answer depends on *which* 50 panels happened to get tested, and a pre-trained encoder is itself a random object — two runs of the same pre-training produce different representations. At *n* = 50 the standard deviation across runs is bigger than several of the gaps you will be comparing. Report the standard deviation next to every mean, and do not read a difference smaller than it.
68	
69	**What each cell averages over.** Use these run counts, so that every submission's table is comparable:
70	
71	| Row | Runs per cell |
72	|---|---|
73	| Ridge on the raw gauges | 5 — one per label draw, `seed=replicate` |
74	| Frozen encoder + ridge | 15 — each of the 3 encoders × 5 label draws |
75	| Frozen random encoder + ridge | 5 — one `random_encoder()` × 5 label draws |
76	| Network from scratch | 5 — one per label draw, `seed=replicate` |
77	| Fine-tuned encoder | 5 — one per label draw, `seed=replicate`, draw *r* starting from encoder *r* mod 3, so all three encoders are used |
78	
79	**Pre-train once per seed, outside your label loop.** Pre-training is the only slow step, about 10 seconds. Nothing about it depends on the labels. Doing it inside the loop turns a two-minute analysis into an hour.
80	
81	**Two evaluation extracts.** Everything you compare is scored on `labeled_dev.csv`. `labeled_test.csv` is scored once, on the single pipeline you recommend. Anything you decide by looking at data is decided on dev.
82	
83	---
84	
85	## Part 1 — One table
86	
87	**Exhibit 1.** Five methods at four label counts, scored on the dev extract, each cell a mean and a standard deviation:
88	
89	1. **Ridge on the 160 raw gauges** — the incumbent.
90	2. **Frozen encoder + ridge** — pre-train on the unlabelled traces, freeze, fit ridge on the representation.
91	3. **Frozen random encoder + ridge** — the control Handout 9 §3.3 requires.
92	4. **Network from scratch.**
93	5. **Fine-tuned encoder.**
94	
95	`starter/kestrel.py` has one function for each. The whole table is two nested loops.
96	
97	Then answer, in the memo:
98	
99	1. **What happens to the incumbent as labels accumulate?** Compare its error at *n* = 50 against *n* = 1000, and against the error you would get by ignoring the gauges entirely and predicting the mean strength. Say what kind of limit this is — a shortage of data, or something else — and how your table tells the two apart.
100	2. **What does pre-training buy, and at which label counts?** Give the comparison against training from scratch at the same *n*.
101	3. **What does the random-encoder row rule out?** State what your table would have meant without it.
102	4. **Where does the ordering change?** Compare the frozen encoder against training from scratch at each label count. Say where the ordering changes, if it does, and where your standard deviations do not let you say. Bracket the crossover — four label counts bracket it, they do not locate it.
103	
104	## Part 2 — The recommendation
105	
106	**`memo.pdf` — at most 2 pages of prose plus Exhibit 1**, addressed to the Head of Quality. Answer her three questions in order:
107	
108	1. **Will more destructive tests fix the current model?** Give the number that settles it.
109	2. **Can the unlabelled traces be made useful?** Say what method you would deploy at Kestrel's current label count, and what error it gives against the incumbent's.
110	3. **How many tests should the next panel family budget?** Give a number, and say what happens on either side of it. Convert it to money at $4,400 per tested panel, against the engineer's proposed 2,000.
111	
112	Then score your recommended pipeline **once** on `labeled_test.csv`, report that number beside its dev counterpart, and note the difference in one sentence.
113	
114	Close with what your evidence does not establish.

118	## Optional extension (up to 4 bonus points)
119	
120	Not required, and a wrong answer cannot lower your score. Pick one.
121	
122	- **Does the pretext task have to be hard?** `pretrain()` takes `mask_fraction`. Try 0.05 and 0.60 alongside the prescribed 0.30 and report what the frozen representation is worth in each case.
123	- **How much unlabelled data do you need?** Pre-train on the first 2,000 traces instead of all 20,000 and report the difference. Say what that implies for a plant that has just installed the instrumentation.
124	- **Beat the incumbent honestly.** The linear model fails for a structural reason. Construct a feature set that fixes it without any pre-training, fit the same ridge on it, and say how close it gets and what you had to know to build it. Keep the model a ridge: the point is the features, not a more flexible learner.

168	## Things that commonly go wrong
169	
170	- **Reporting one run.** The protocol asks for three pre-training seeds and five label draws. At *n* = 50 a single run tells you almost nothing.
171	- **Reading a difference smaller than its standard deviation.** Some of the comparisons in this table are not resolvable at *n* = 50. Saying so scores better than picking a winner.
172	- **Pre-training inside the label loop.** This is the difference between two minutes and an hour.
173	- **Selecting on the test extract.** Compare on dev. Score once on test, on one pipeline.
174	- **Reporting the study and never answering the question.** The Head of Quality asked for a budget number.

192	## How marks are typically lost
193	
194	None of these is a trick. All are recoverable by re-reading the brief before you submit.
195	
196	- **The table without the control.** Criterion 1 asks for a specific extra row and the brief says which handout section requires it. A table that omits it cannot support the claim it is being used to make, and cannot score above half marks here.
197	- **One pre-training run.** A pre-trained encoder is a random object; two runs of the same procedure give different representations. The protocol says three, and says to average.
198	- **Reading a difference smaller than its standard deviation.** At the smallest label count several rows overlap. Reporting an ordering the experiment cannot resolve is worse than reporting that it cannot resolve it.
199	- **Announcing a crossover to the decimal.** Four label counts bracket a crossover. They do not locate one.
200	- **Diagnosing the incumbent as short of data.** Criterion 2 asks what kind of limit it is hitting. The table contains the evidence that settles it; use it rather than asserting.
201	- **Explaining the incumbent's failure without reference to the process.** The data dictionary records what Process Engineering says about how strength arises. A good answer connects the shape of the failure to that description.
202	- **Selecting on the test extract.** Choosing the method or the label count by looking at it is a criterion 4 deduction even when the number is right. So is scoring several pipelines on it and reporting the best.
203	- **Pre-training inside the label loop.** Not a criterion by itself, but it is where nearly all the reported pain on this assignment comes from.
204	- **A memo that reports the study and never answers the question.** The Head of Quality asked whether to spend $8.8 million. An exhibit and no number is a criterion 3 failure regardless of how good the exhibits are.
205	- **A generic AI process note.** "Used AI to help write code, verified output" earns nothing under criterion 5.
206	# Kestrel Composites — data dictionary
207	
208	Extract prepared by Process Engineering, September 2026.
209	
210	**Grain.** One row per cured panel.
211	
212	---
213	
214	## The gauges (160 columns, identical in every file)
215	
216	Every panel is cured in an autoclave instrumented with 160 gauges. All 160 are logged automatically for every panel, whether or not that panel is ever tested.
217	
218	| Block | Columns | What it reads |
219	|---|---|---|
220	| Oven zone temperature | `cure_temp_z01` … `cure_temp_z40` | Thermocouples distributed through the oven, °C |
221	| Tool pressure | `press_p01` … `press_p32` | Pressure taps under the vacuum bag, kPa |
222	| Resin flow | `resin_flow_f01` … `resin_flow_f32` | Flow-front gauges around the tool, arbitrary units |
223	| Dielectric cure monitor | `dielectric_d01` … `dielectric_d32` | Ion-viscosity probes tracking the cure reaction |
224	| Vacuum line | `vacuum_v01` … `vacuum_v24` | Line pressures at the bag ports, kPa |
225	
226	The gauges are **highly redundant**. They are 160 different views of a much smaller number of underlying process conditions — how hot the part actually got, how fast it got there, how completely the resin flowed, how much contamination was present. Two gauges on opposite sides of the same oven zone tell you nearly the same thing. This redundancy is why a gauge that drops out can be reconstructed from the others, and it is worth keeping in mind when you look at what pre-training does.
227	
228	## The identifier and the target
229	
230	| Column | Definition |
231	|---|---|
232	| `panel_id` | Panel identifier, unique across all four files. The prefix says which file a panel is in: `TR` train, `DV` dev, `TS` test, `UL` unlabelled. |
233	| `strength_mpa` | **Target.** Interlaminar shear strength, MPa. Measured by loading the panel to failure in a press. Present only in the three `labeled_*` files. |
234	
235	Measuring it destroys the panel. That is the whole problem: a labelled row costs a saleable part plus about four hours of lab time, and an unlabelled row costs nothing at all.
236	
237	**A note on negative values.** About 1–2% of labelled panels show a strength below zero, which no real panel can have. Like every dataset in this course, this extract is simulated, and those values come from the simulation's severe-contamination term rather than from a measurement. Leave them in: they are the badly delaminated panels, and the prescribed models and every comparison in the brief are computed with them included.
238	
239	## What Process Engineering says about strength
240	
241	> Strength needs two things to go right at once. The resin has to flow far enough to wet out every ply, and the cure has to run far enough to convert the matrix. A panel that is beautifully wetted but under-cured is weak. A panel that is fully cured but resin-starved is weak in a different way. **You cannot make up for a deficit in one with a surplus in the other** — the two failure modes multiply rather than add.
242	>
243	> Separately, contamination above a threshold causes delamination. Below the threshold it does nothing measurable; above it, strength falls away sharply.
244	
245	That paragraph is a description of the physics, not a hint about modelling. It is here because it is what the process engineers would tell you, and it is relevant to at least one thing you will observe.
246	
247	---
248	
249	## The files
250	
251	| File | Rows | Labelled | Use |
252	|---|---|---|---|
253	| `labeled_train.csv` | 2,000 | yes | fitting |
254	| `labeled_dev.csv` | 1,000 | yes | every comparison you make |
255	| `labeled_test.csv` | 1,000 | yes | scored once, at the end |
256	| `unlabeled_traces.csv.gz` | 20,000 | no | pre-training |
257	
258	All four come from the same autoclave and the same period. No panel appears in more than one file. The unlabelled file is gzipped; `pandas.read_csv` opens it directly, and `starter/kestrel.py` already does.
259	
260	`dev` and `test` are interchangeable except in what you are allowed to do with them: `dev` is where you compare things, `test` is scored once on whatever you end up recommending. They are not equally hard — `var(y)` is about 10% lower on `test` — so expect a small difference and report it rather than accounting for it.
261	# How to approach the assignments
262	
263	**IDS 575: Machine Learning and Statistical Methods for Business Analytics · Fall 2026**

268	## 1. What is being graded
269	
270	You have a coding agent (`05_setting_up_your_agent.md`). It can write a modeling pipeline faster
271	than you can describe one, so writing the pipeline is not the skill being assessed.
272	
273	What is assessed is the part that stays yours:
274	
275	- deciding what question is actually being asked
276	- noticing when an answer is too good
277	- knowing what evidence would settle a disagreement
278	- saying what the evidence does and does not support
279	
280	The broad goal of these assignments is to help you become comfortable working with AI to define and implement machine learning pipelines in a business context. To do that, you need a certain level of competency in the core concepts of machine learning. And imparting that competency is the broad goal of the course. 
281	
282	Each assignment is preparation for an in-person exam where you will have none of these tools. If you
283	finish an assignment and could not explain your headline number on paper, it has not done its job.
284	
285	---
286	
287	## 2. What every assignment looks like
288	
289	A business situation, a dataset, and **an analysis someone else has already done** — an analyst, a
290	contractor, an engineer. That analysis is plausible, arithmetically correct, but also wrong. Your task is
291	not "build a model." It is "understand what is wrong, why it is wrong, establish what is true, and say what should be done."
292	
293	Four things are submitted every time:
294	
295	| | |
296	|---|---|
297	| `memo.pdf` or `memo.md` | To a named business reader. Length limit stated per assignment, and enforced. |
298	| `analysis/` | Your code. Runs end to end from one command. |
299	| `ai_process_note.md` | One page. What you delegated, what you rejected, how you checked. |
300	| `sessions/` | Complete exported history of every AI session used. |
301	
302	---
303	
304	## 3. A working order that tends to go well
305	
306	**Read the brief and the data dictionary yourself first.** The dictionaries record how each column
307	is produced and *when*. That timing information decides which columns you may use, and it is easier
308	to take in before a model exists to distract you.
309	
310	**Write down what you expect before you compute anything.** What is the base rate? What order of
311	magnitude should the effect be? What would a suspiciously good result look like? Two minutes of this
312	is what makes you able to be surprised, and being surprised is how you find things.
313	
314	**Get a baseline before you get a model.** Every assignment has a do-nothing answer — predict the
315	majority class, predict the mean, keep the current price. Compute it. It is the denominator for
316	everything that follows and the number most often missing from an agent's output.
317	
318	**Change one thing at a time.** Where an assignment asks for an audit trail — one row per problem,
319	one fix, and the resulting number — build it as you go rather than reconstructing it at the end. It
320	is also your best defence against an agent that quietly fixed three things at once.
321	
322	---
323	
324	## 4. Working with your agent
325	
326	The assignments are graded lightly, and in principle, you can delegate the majority of work to AI. However, this goes against the course's learning goals and will make you struggle in the in-person assessments. Hence, the following strategy is recommended for optimal learning.
327	
328	**Delegate the work, not the judgment.** Good to hand over: "write a grouped cross-validation split
329	by member_id", "sweep the ridge penalty over the grid and plot train and validation error". Not good
330	to hand over: "tell me whether this model is good enough to deploy", "write the recommendation."
331	The second list is the assignment.
332	
333	**Give it the business context, not just the file.** An agent told "predict churn from this CSV" will
334	optimise accuracy. An agent told what an offer costs and what a retained member is worth will do
335	something quite different. The context is in the brief; pass it along.
336	
337	**Ask it to argue against itself.** "What would have to be true for this estimate to be wrong?" and
338	"What is the strongest objection to this conclusion?" are the two highest-yield prompts in the course.
339	
340	**Be suspicious of agreement.** If the first answer confirms what you expected and nothing errored,
341	slow down rather than speed up.
342	
343	**Do not let it choose the evaluation design.** Splits, metrics, units of analysis, and what counts as
344	held out are the graded content of this course. An agent will pick a sensible default, and these
345	datasets are built to punish sensible defaults.
346	
347	**If you do not understand what it produced, stop.** Get it explained or throw it out. You are
348	responsible for every line and may be asked in class to explain any of it.
349	
350	**Export your session before you close it** (`03_exporting_your_session_history.md`). The Codex app
351	copies to the clipboard rather than to a file, so paste it somewhere immediately.
352	
353	---
354	
355	## 5. The memo
356	
357	Written to a named person who has a decision to make and will read the first paragraph carefully and
358	the rest quickly.
359	
360	- **Lead with the recommendation.** Not the method, not the data cleaning.
361	- **Give the number, then the number it replaces.** "The honest estimate is X, not the Y in the
362	  current proposal, and the gap is mostly Z."
363	- **Quantify the uncertainty once, plainly, and move on.** A memo that never commits is not useful.
364	- **State conditions so someone could check them.** "Deploy if corporate accounts stay under 15% of
365	  the book" is a recommendation. "Deploy with caution" is not.
366	- **Respect the length limit.** Exhibits do not count against prose length; prose does.
367	
368	---
369	
370	## 6. Before you submit
371	
372	Full list in `04_submission_checklist.md`. The five that matter most:
373	
374	- [ ] The analysis runs end to end, from a clean copy of the folder, with one command.
375	- [ ] Every number in the memo comes from that run.
376	- [ ] Every session is exported into `sessions/`, complete and unedited.
377	- [ ] The process note names specific things you rejected or corrected. If you rejected nothing all
378	      assignment, think about that before writing it down.
379	- [ ] You can explain any part of the submission out loud, without notes.
380	
381	That last item is not decorative. You may be asked to explain or modify a piece of your submitted
382	work in a short oral check. 
383	# Policy on generative AI and coding agents
384	
385	**IDS 575: Machine Learning and Statistical Methods for Business Analytics · Fall 2026**
386	
387	This policy governs the three take-home assignments. It supplements, and does not replace, the university's academic integrity policy.
388	
389	---
390	
391	## The short version
392	
393	**On assignments, use one of the two approved agents freely, and disclose completely.**
394	**In the exam room, use nothing.**
395	**You own everything you submit.**
396	
397	---
398	
399	## 1. Why the policy is written this way
400	
401	You will graduate into work where directing an AI system through an analysis is ordinary. Pretending otherwise in a graduate business course would be a disservice. So the assignments are AI-enabled by design, and they are built to help you become comfortable in working with AI in designing and implementing Machine Learning pipelines.
402	
403	The trade is that the assignments carry 30% of the grade — 10% each — and the in-person exams carry the other 70%. The assignments are where you learn; the exams are where independent understanding is evidenced. They are also built on the same material as the exam that follows each of them, so treating an assignment as something to get past rather than something to learn from costs twice: once at 10%, and again on the exam it was preparation for.
404	
405	---
406	
407	## 1a. The approved agents
408	
409	**This course uses one of two coding agents: the Codex app or Claude Code. No other coding agent may
410	be used on coursework.**
411	
412	Both produce a complete, exportable session history, which is the property the course requires and
413	is not universal among these tools. Standardizing on two means the setup instructions apply to
414	everyone, the transcripts are in formats I can read quickly, and help in class applies to the whole
415	room.
416	
417	**Codex has a free path** — the Free plan plus the $100 student credit grant OpenAI makes available
418	to verified students at US and Canadian universities — so nobody needs to spend money to complete an
419	assignment. Claude Code requires a Claude plan that includes it. Setup for both, and how to claim
420	the grant, is in `05_setting_up_your_agent.md`.
421	
422	
423	
424	## 2. Permitted
425	
426	- Using the Codex app or Claude Code on any part of a take-home assignment.
427	- Asking for explanations, code, debugging help, alternative approaches, critique of your reasoning, and critique of your writing.
428	- Using either approved agent, for many sessions across many days.
429	- Using AI to help you draft the memo, provided the judgments in it are yours and you can defend them.
430	- Discussing course concepts with classmates.
431	
432	There is no expectation that you minimise your AI use, and no credit for having used less of it.
433	
434	## 3. Required
435	
436	**Work inside the assignment folder.** Each assignment ships as a bounded folder. Keep your work there.
437	
438	**Export the complete session history for every AI session you use, and submit all of it.** Not a summary, not the interesting parts, not one representative session. If you opened five sessions, all five are submitted. `03_exporting_your_session_history.md` explains how, for each supported tool.
439	
440	**Validate outputs.** Every number in your memo must be reproducible from your submitted code. If your agent reported a figure you cannot regenerate, it does not go in the memo.
441	
442	**Document your corrections.** The AI process note asks what you delegated, what you changed or rejected, and how you checked the result. This is the part of the submission that most directly evidences your judgment, and it is graded on specificity.
443	
444	**Be able to explain and modify your work.** You may be asked, in class or in a short oral check, to walk through a piece of your submission or make a small change to it. This applies to every line you submit regardless of who or what wrote it.
445	
446	## 4. Not permitted
447	
448	- **Any generative AI, internet access, or communication device during the in-person midterms and final.** Permitted materials will be announced in advance.
449	- **Using any coding agent other than the Codex app or Claude Code** on assignments.
450	- **Concealing AI use, or using a tool whose sessions you do not disclose.**
451	- **Editing, truncating, or reconstructing a transcript** to change what it shows. Submitting a hand-written "transcript" of a session you did not save is fabrication, not a formatting shortcut.
452	- **Sharing or receiving code, memos, prompt logs, completed folders, or final answers.** The assignments are individual. Discussing concepts is encouraged; exchanging artifacts is not.
453	- **Submitting work you cannot explain.**
454	- **Entering passwords, API keys, or confidential personal or employer data into an AI tool.** All course data is synthetic and safe to share with a model. Your own material may not be.
455	
456	---
457	
458	## 5. What the transcripts are, and are not
459	
460	**They are an audit trail, not proof of understanding.** A long transcript does not earn marks and a short one does not lose them. The instructor may review logs selectively — typically when a submission's quality and its process note do not match each other, or when a memo contains a claim the submitted code does not produce.
461	
462	**They are not a second deliverable.** Do not curate them, annotate them, or write them for an audience. Export and attach.
463	
464	**They are read alongside your process note.** The most common signal of a problem is not a transcript showing heavy AI use; it is a transcript showing that a conclusion arrived fully formed and was never questioned, paired with a process note claiming careful validation.
465	
466	---
467	
468	## 6. If an export goes wrong
469	
470	Both approved agents produce a complete session history, so the usual cause of a gap is a mechanical
471	one: a clipboard copy that did not land, a session closed before it was saved, a transcript that
472	expired. That is recoverable if you say so and unrecoverable if you do not.
473	
474	If a session you used is missing or incomplete:
475	
476	1. Submit whatever you do have.
477	2. Add a short note in `sessions/README.md` stating which sessions are affected, roughly how many,
478	   what is missing, and what you used them for.
479	3. Export at the end of every working session from then on, so it does not happen twice.
480	
481	A disclosed gap is fine. An undisclosed one is a violation.
482	
483	---
484	
485	## 7. Privacy warning, read this once
486	
487	Session transcripts from Codex and Claude Code **embed the full content of files the agent read and the full output of commands it ran**. If you work on assignment material in a directory that also contains something private, that private material can end up inside the transcript you submit.
488	
489	Do the assignments in a clean folder. Before submitting, open your export and look at it. You are responsible for what is in it.
490	
491	---
492	
493	## 8. Consequences
494	
495	Concealed AI use, fabricated or edited transcripts, and shared artefacts are academic integrity violations and are referred through the university process. Because each assignment is worth 10%, the cost of a violation is enormously out of proportion to anything it could gain. There is no version of these assignments where dishonesty is the rational choice.
496	
497	If you are unsure whether something is permitted, ask before you do it. Asking has never cost anyone marks in this course.
498	# Exporting your AI session history
499	
500	**IDS 575: Machine Learning and Statistical Methods for Business Analytics · Fall 2026**
501	
502	Every assignment requires the complete exported history of every AI session you used. This sheet
503	explains how, for both approved agents.
504	
505	> **Export at the end of each working session, not at the end of the assignment.** Both tools have
506	> some way of losing history — a retention window, a clipboard that chokes on a long conversation.
507	> If you wait until the night before the deadline, some of what you need may no longer exist.
508	
509	> **Before you submit, open your export and read it.** Agent transcripts embed the full contents of
510	> files the agent read and the full output of commands it ran. Work in a clean folder that contains
511	> only course material.
512	
513	---
514	
515	## What goes in `sessions/`
516	
517	```
518	sessions/
519	  README.md              which agent, how many sessions, anything the export omits
520	  codex/                 one file per session
521	  claude-code/           one file per session
522	```
523	
524	You will normally have only one of those two subfolders. `sessions/README.md` is required either way
525	and can be three lines.
526	
527	---
528	
529	## 1. Codex
530	
531	### The app
532	
533	Open the session, use **Copy as Markdown** from the conversation menu, and paste into a file:
534	
535	```
536	sessions/codex/a1-session-1.md
537	```
538	
539	That is the whole procedure. Name the files in the order you worked; the names do not matter beyond
540	being distinguishable.
541	
542	Two cautions:
543	
544	- **It goes to the clipboard, not to a file.** Paste it somewhere immediately. A plain text editor is
545	  safer than Word, which has been reported to struggle with very long conversations.
546	- **Do it per session, while the session is open.** There is no bulk export.
547	
548	### The CLI
549	
550	Inside a session, `/copy` puts the conversation on the clipboard; paste it into a `.md` file the same
551	way.
552	
553	### The transcript on disk — your backup
554	
555	Codex also writes a full rollout file per session:
556	
557	```
558	~/.codex/sessions/YYYY/MM/DD/rollout-<timestamp>-<session-uuid>.jsonl
559	```
560	
561	Copy them if you want a belt-and-braces record:
562	
563	```bash
564	mkdir -p sessions/codex
565	cp ~/.codex/sessions/2026/09/11/rollout-*.jsonl sessions/codex/
566	```
567	
568	This is the complete log — more complete than the Markdown copy, which renders the conversation
569	rather than recording every tool call. **The Markdown is what I ask for. The JSONL is what saves you
570	if the Markdown copy failed and you did not notice.** Submitting both is fine and never penalised.
571	
572	Two settings to check before you start:
573	
574	- If `~/.codex/config.toml` contains `[history] persistence = "none"`, your history is being
575	  suppressed. Set it back to `"save-all"` (the default).
576	- Do not run assignment work with `--ephemeral`, which skips session persistence.
577	
578	**Check the size before you attach.** Rollout files can get large, because they store repeated
579	context snapshots and raw tool output:
580	
581	```bash
582	du -h sessions/codex/*
583	```
584	
585	If the folder is over about 50 MB, zip it and say so in `sessions/README.md`.
586	
587	---
588	
589	## 2. Claude Code
590	
591	### Option A — the raw transcript
592	
593	Transcripts are stored as JSONL at:
594	
595	```
596	~/.claude/projects/<encoded-project-path>/<session-id>.jsonl
597	```
598	
599	`<encoded-project-path>` is your working directory with every non-alphanumeric character replaced by
600	`-`. Run `/status` inside a session to get the session ID; that ID is the filename. To see every
601	session you have, `claude --resume` opens an interactive picker.
602	
603	### Option B — the readable export
604	
605	From inside a session: `/export sessions/claude-code/a1-session-1.txt`
606	
607	### Retention
608	
609	Claude Code deletes transcripts after **30 days** by default. Copy the file into your assignment
610	folder at the end of each session rather than relying on the retention setting.
611	
612	---

616	Ordinary case:
617

619	# AI sessions for Assignment 1
620	
621	Agent used: Codex app (4 sessions)
622	
623	- codex/ : 4 Markdown exports, complete. Rollout JSONL for the same four sessions

643	Both tools change quickly. If a path or a menu item on this sheet is not where it says it is,

658	
659	```
660	lastname_firstname_a1/
661	  memo.pdf                  or memo.md
662	  analysis/
663	    run.sh                  or run.py — the one command
664	    README.md               what to run, what it produces, roughly how long
665	    <your code>

674

676	
677	## The four pieces
678	
679	### `memo.pdf`
680	
681	Addressed to the business reader named in the assignment. Length limits are per assignment (see each brief; A1 carries two memo sections, A3 allows 3 pages) plus the stated number of exhibits. Exhibits do not count against the prose limit.
682	
683	Lead with the recommendation. Give the number and the number it replaces. State conditions in a form someone could check.
684	
685	### `analysis/`
686	
687	Must run end to end on a clean copy of the assignment folder with **one command**. State the command in `analysis/README.md`. If it takes more than about ten minutes, say so and say why.
688	
689	Assume the grader has Python 3.10+, numpy, pandas, scikit-learn and matplotlib and nothing else. If you need something further, list it in `analysis/README.md`. Do not require a GPU.
690	
691	Every number in your memo must come from this run.
692	
693	### `ai_process_note.md`
694	
695	One page maximum. Three things:
696	
697	1. **What you delegated.** The substantive tasks, not "helped with code."
698	2. **What you changed or rejected, and why.** Specific instances. If you rejected nothing at all across an entire assignment, say so and say why you think that was.
699	3. **How you checked the final numbers.** What you recomputed, what you compared against, what you would still not bet on.
700	
701	Generic notes score zero on this criterion. "Used Claude Code to write the analysis, reviewed the output, verified it was correct" is a generic note.
702	
703	### `sessions/`
704	
705	Complete exported history of every AI session used, per `03_exporting_your_session_history.md`, with a `README.md` naming the agent and disclosing anything the exports omit.
706

735	
736	- [ ] Every session exported
737	- [ ] Exports are unedited
738	- [ ] `sessions/README.md` names the agent and any gaps
739	- [ ] You have opened the export and confirmed it contains nothing private

742	
743	- [ ] You can explain any part of the submission out loud, without notes

827	
828	## 5. Staying inside the budget
829	
830	Free-plan usage plus the grant covers the three assignments comfortably, but that assumes you are
831	not wasting it. Four habits, in order of how much they matter:
832	
833	**Never let the agent read a data file into the conversation.** `member_months.csv` is 33,000 rows.
834	Pasting it, or letting the agent `cat` it, can burn more of your allowance in one message than a
835	whole working session should. Have the agent *write code that reads the file* and report back the
836	numbers. The data dictionaries are short and are meant to be read; the CSVs are not.
837	
838	**Match the model to the task.** Use a cheaper model for routine work — writing a loop, fixing an
839	import, reformatting a table. Save the strongest model for the things that need it: debugging
840	something you do not understand, or arguing with you about an evaluation design. The difference in
841	cost between the top and bottom models is more than twentyfold, and most of what you will ask for
842	does not need the top one.
843	
844	**Start a new session for each work block, and keep it on one topic.** A single session that runs
845	all week re-sends its whole history with every message. Three focused sessions cost far less than
846	one sprawling one, and they are easier to export and easier for me to read.
847	
848	**Don't re-run the expensive things.** Cache what you compute. `analyst_model.py` produces the same
849	numbers every time; run it once and save the output rather than asking the agent to re-run it in
850	every session.
851

"""
Assignment 2 starter -- Kestrel Composites.

Everything you need is here.  You should not have to write a neural network,
a training loop, or a masking routine; you should have to decide what to run,
read the results, and say what they mean.

    from kestrel import *

    Xtr, ytr = load("train")          # gauges (standardised), strength
    Xdev, ydev = load("dev")
    traces = load("traces")           # unlabeled, standardised, no y

    enc = pretrain(traces, seed=0)    # self-supervised, ~10 s
    print(frozen_ridge(enc, Xtr[:100], ytr[:100], Xdev, ydev))

Five things you can do to the data, and nothing else:

    ridge(Xtr, ytr, Xte, yte)             a regularized linear model
    pretrain(pool, seed)                  masked reconstruction -> an encoder
    random_encoder(seed)                  an encoder that was never trained
    frozen_ridge(enc, ...)                freeze the encoder, ridge on top
    supervised(Xtr, ytr, Xte, yte, seed)  train a network end to end,
                                          from scratch or from an encoder

All five return a test MSE on whatever evaluation set you pass, except
`pretrain` and `random_encoder`, which return an encoder.
"""
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

from mlp import MLP

DATA = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1] / "data"
TARGET = "strength_mpa"
ID = "panel_id"

FILES = {"train": "labeled_train.csv", "dev": "labeled_dev.csv",
         "test": "labeled_test.csv", "traces": "unlabeled_traces.csv.gz"}

# ---- the protocol, fixed by the brief ------------------------------------
MASK_FRACTION = 0.30      # share of gauges hidden at each pre-training step
ENCODER_SHAPE = (64, 16)  # hidden layers; the representation is the first
PRETRAIN_EPOCHS = 40
PRETRAIN_LR = 3e-3
PRETRAIN_BATCH = 256
HEAD_WIDTH = 64
SCRATCH_LR = 2e-3
FINETUNE_LR = 1e-3        # reduced, as Handout 9 S3.2 prescribes
MAX_EPOCHS = 800
BATCH = 32
PATIENCE = 60
VAL_FRACTION = 0.25
RIDGE_ALPHAS = np.logspace(-2, 5, 40)

LABEL_COUNTS = (50, 100, 250, 1000)
N_REPLICATES = 5       # independent label draws per cell
N_ENCODER_SEEDS = 3    # independent pre-training runs per cell

_STATS = None


def _standardizer():
    """Centre and scale using the TRAINING gauges only.  Computed once."""
    global _STATS
    if _STATS is None:
        raw = pd.read_csv(DATA / FILES["train"])
        G = raw.drop(columns=[ID, TARGET]).to_numpy(float)
        _STATS = (G.mean(0), G.std(0) + 1e-9)
    return _STATS


def load(which):
    """load('train') -> (X, y).   load('traces') -> X.

    X is always standardised with the training-set statistics, so every matrix
    you touch is on the same scale.
    """
    if which not in FILES:
        raise KeyError(f"unknown file {which!r}; options: {sorted(FILES)}")
    df = pd.read_csv(DATA / FILES[which])
    mu, sd = _standardizer()
    X = (df.drop(columns=[c for c in (ID, TARGET) if c in df.columns])
           .to_numpy(float) - mu) / sd
    if TARGET in df.columns:
        return X, df[TARGET].to_numpy(float)
    return X


def gauge_names():
    return [c for c in pd.read_csv(DATA / FILES["train"], nrows=1).columns
            if c not in (ID, TARGET)]


def label_subset(n, replicate):
    """The indices of the n labelled panels for one replicate.

    The brief asks for N_REPLICATES independent draws at each label count,
    because with 50 labels the answer depends on WHICH 50 you happened to
    test.  These indices are fixed by (n, replicate), so everyone's table is
    comparable and yours reproduces.
    """
    rng = np.random.default_rng(9000 + 100 * replicate + n)
    n_train = len(pd.read_csv(DATA / FILES["train"], usecols=[ID]))
    return rng.choice(n_train, n, replace=False)


# ---------------------------------------------------------------- the models
def ridge(Xtr, ytr, Xte, yte, seed=0):
    """Ridge regression.  Penalty chosen on a 75/25 split of the labels."""
    Xtr, Xte = np.asarray(Xtr, float), np.asarray(Xte, float)
    A = np.hstack([Xtr, np.ones((len(Xtr), 1))])
    B = np.hstack([Xte, np.ones((len(Xte), 1))])
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    o = rng.permutation(len(A))
    cut = max(12, int(0.75 * len(A)))
    fit, val = o[:cut], o[cut:]
    I = np.eye(A.shape[1])
    best, best_a = np.inf, RIDGE_ALPHAS[0]
    for a in RIDGE_ALPHAS:
        W = np.linalg.solve(A[fit].T @ A[fit] + a * I, A[fit].T @ ytr[fit])
        e = np.mean((A[val] @ W - ytr[val]) ** 2)
        if e < best:
            best, best_a = e, a
    W = np.linalg.solve(A.T @ A + best_a * I, A.T @ ytr)
    return float(np.mean((B @ W - yte) ** 2))


def pretrain(pool, seed=0, epochs=PRETRAIN_EPOCHS, mask_fraction=MASK_FRACTION):
    """Self-supervised pre-training: hide gauges, rebuild them.

    No labels are used or needed.  A fresh set of gauges is hidden at every
    epoch -- that re-drawing is what forces the network to learn the process
    rather than memorise one corruption.

    Returns the encoder.  Pre-train ONCE per pool and reuse it; it is by far
    the most expensive thing here (~10 seconds) and nothing about it depends on
    the labels.
    """
    pool = np.asarray(pool, float)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    net = MLP([pool.shape[1], *ENCODER_SHAPE, pool.shape[1]], seed=seed)
    for ep in range(epochs):
        corrupted = pool.copy()
        corrupted[rng.random(pool.shape) < mask_fraction] = 0.0
        net.fit(corrupted, pool, epochs=1, batch_size=PRETRAIN_BATCH,
                lr=PRETRAIN_LR, seed=seed * 1000 + ep)
    return net


def random_encoder(seed=99):
    """An encoder of identical shape whose weights were never trained.

    Handout 9 S3.3: without this you cannot tell 'pre-training learned
    something' from 'this architecture makes useful random features'.
    """
    n = len(gauge_names())
    return MLP([n, *ENCODER_SHAPE, n], seed=seed)


def representation(enc, X):
    """The learned features: the encoder's first hidden layer, 64 numbers.

    160 gauges in, 64 learned features out.  Handout 9 S3.4 is about which
    layer to take; the brief fixes it at the first so that everyone's table
    is comparable.
    """
    return enc.hidden(np.asarray(X, float), layer=1)


def frozen_ridge(enc, Xtr, ytr, Xte, yte, seed=0):
    """Freeze the encoder, fit ridge on its representation.  Handout 9 S2.1."""
    return ridge(representation(enc, Xtr), ytr,
                 representation(enc, Xte), yte, seed=seed)


def supervised(Xtr, ytr, Xte, yte, seed=0, encoder=None):
    """Train a network end to end and return its test MSE.

    encoder=None  -> from scratch, at SCRATCH_LR.
    encoder=enc   -> fine-tuning: start from the pre-trained weights and train
                     everything at the reduced FINETUNE_LR.

    The target is centred before fitting and the mean added back afterwards.
    Without that the output layer starts far from the data and, with only 50
    labels and early stopping, never gets there.
    """
    Xtr, Xte = np.asarray(Xtr, float), np.asarray(Xte, float)
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    o = rng.permutation(len(Xtr))
    cut = max(12, int((1 - VAL_FRACTION) * len(Xtr)))
    fit, val = o[:cut], o[cut:]
    centre = ytr.mean()
    net = MLP([Xtr.shape[1], HEAD_WIDTH, 1], seed=seed)
    if encoder is not None:
        net.copy_body_from(encoder)
    net.fit(Xtr[fit], ytr[fit] - centre, epochs=MAX_EPOCHS, batch_size=BATCH,
            lr=(SCRATCH_LR if encoder is None else FINETUNE_LR), seed=seed,
            X_val=Xtr[val], Y_val=ytr[val] - centre, patience=PATIENCE)
    return float(np.mean((net.predict(Xte).ravel() + centre - yte) ** 2))


if __name__ == "__main__":
    Xtr, ytr = load("train")
    Xdev, ydev = load("dev")
    print(f"train {Xtr.shape}   dev {Xdev.shape}   "
          f"traces {load('traces').shape}")
    print(f"strength: mean {ytr.mean():.1f}  var(dev) {ydev.var():.1f}")
    print("\nsmoke test (n=100, one replicate):")
    i = label_subset(100, 0)
    print(f"  ridge on the 160 gauges    {ridge(Xtr[i], ytr[i], Xdev, ydev):7.1f}")
    enc = pretrain(load("traces"), seed=0)
    print(f"  frozen encoder + ridge     {frozen_ridge(enc, Xtr[i], ytr[i], Xdev, ydev):7.1f}")
    print(f"  frozen random + ridge      "
          f"{frozen_ridge(random_encoder(), Xtr[i], ytr[i], Xdev, ydev):7.1f}")
    print(f"  network from scratch       {supervised(Xtr[i], ytr[i], Xdev, ydev, 0):7.1f}")

## How the protocol works

**The setup.** Kestrel has 2,000 tested panels. The question is how each method would do if Kestrel had only 50, 100, 250 or 1,000 of them. So we pretend we have fewer labels than we do, at each of those four **label counts**. Every model is always scored on the same 1,000 dev panels. Only the training set changes.

**What a "label draw" is.** Say n = 50. There are many different sets of 50 panels you could pick out of the 2,000, and the answer depends on which 50 you get. One run would mix up how good the method is with how lucky the sample was. So at each n you take **5 different random subsets** of size n and fit on each one. Each subset is a "draw" (also called a replicate).

`label_subset(n, replicate)` in [kestrel.py:96-107](starter/kestrel.py#L96-L107) does this. For replicate r = 0…4 it returns the row indices of n training panels. The random seed is fixed at `9000 + 100*r + n`, so every student gets exactly the same panels and the table is comparable across submissions.

One detail: draws at different n are **not nested**. The seed depends on n, so draw 0 at n = 100 does not contain draw 0 at n = 50. Each label count is a fresh sample.

**The second source of randomness: pre-training seeds.** This one has nothing to do with labels. The encoder is trained on the 20,000 unlabelled traces, and two pre-training runs with different seeds give different encoders. The brief has you train **3 encoders once, before any loops**, and reuse them everywhere. Pre-training never sees a label, so retraining it inside the loop would just waste about 10 seconds per call.

**How the runs fill each cell.** A cell is one method at one n. Its mean ± SD is taken over these runs:

| Method | Runs | Which runs |
|---|---|---|
| Ridge, raw gauges | 5 | draws 0–4 |
| Frozen pre-trained + ridge | 15 | 3 encoders × 5 draws |
| Frozen random + ridge | 5 | 1 untrained encoder × 5 draws |
| From scratch | 5 | draws 0–4 |
| Fine-tuned | 5 | draw r starts from encoder r mod 3 (encoders 0,1,2,0,1) |

The frozen row gets 15 runs because it carries both kinds of randomness. That way its SD shows both "which panels" and "which encoder."

Altogether: 3 pre-trainings, then 4 label counts × 35 fits = 140 fits.

**What "seed=replicate" means.** It is a separate thing from the draw. Inside each fit there is a small internal split:
- **Ridge** keeps 25% of its n labels aside to choose the penalty.
- **The networks** hold out 25% for early stopping, and the seed also sets the starting weights.

`seed=replicate` controls that internal randomness. The draw decides which panels you get, and the seed decides how they are split and initialised. One thing to notice: at n = 50, a network trains on only 37 panels and early-stops on 13.

**Why the SDs matter.** The brief warns that at n = 50 the spread across runs is larger than some of the differences between methods. A gap smaller than the SD can't be read as a real difference. That's why the crossover question asks for a bracket ("somewhere between 100 and 250"), not a point.

## Before we start

1. **The frozen rows' internal seed.** The brief says `seed=replicate` for ridge, scratch and fine-tune, but doesn't say what seed the two frozen rows pass to their ridge. `seed=replicate` is the natural choice to match the others, but it's your call.
2. **Before computing anything,** the course guide (§3) asks you to write down what you expect, for example: will the incumbent improve much between n = 50 and n = 1000? Read the "What Process Engineering says about strength" paragraph in [DATA_DICTIONARY.md](data/DATA_DICTIONARY.md) before you answer. The rubric explicitly looks for it.

Next steps could be your A1 summary, setting up the A2 notes, or running the smoke test (`python3 starter/kestrel.py`) to check the environment. Which would you like?

## How these were exported, and why not with `/export`

`03_exporting_your_session_history.md` gives two options for Claude Code:
Option A, the raw JSONL at `~/.claude/projects/<encoded-path>/<session-id>.jsonl`,
and Option B, `/export` from inside a session.

**Option B is not available in the VS Code extension.** Running
`/export sessions/claude-code/a1-session-1.txt` there returns "/export isn't
available in this environment". The `claude` CLI has no `export` subcommand
either (checked against `claude --help` on 2026-09-17, CLI version 2.52-era
build). So, per the sheet's closing instruction to find the equivalent and say
what was done instead:

1. **Option A, unchanged.** The raw transcript is copied verbatim to
   `claude-code/a1-session-N.jsonl`. This is the complete record.
2. **Option B, reproduced.** `render_transcript.py` in this folder renders that
   JSONL as readable text at `claude-code/a1-session-N.txt`. It writes out every
   user and assistant message, every tool call with its arguments, and every
   tool result in full, with nothing truncated. Run it with:

       python sessions/render_transcript.py \
           sessions/claude-code/a1-session-1.jsonl \
           sessions/claude-code/a1-session-1.txt

Both files are submitted. The JSONL is authoritative; the `.txt` is for reading.

## Known gap

Each transcript is copied from disk near the end of its session, so it stops a
few messages short of the true end. The missing tail is the export and the
`git commit`/`git push` that followed it, which are visible in the repository
history. Nothing about the analysis is lost this way.

## Images in the readable rendering

The agent read the course handout PDFs page by page, so the raw transcripts
embed those pages as base64 images. In `a1-session-4.jsonl` they were 93% of
the rendered text, which made the readable `.txt` unreadable -- the opposite
of what it is for.

`render_transcript.py` therefore writes an image as a labelled placeholder
giving its media type and payload size, for example:

    [image omitted from the readable rendering: image/png, 412,336 base64
     chars; the full payload is in the .jsonl]

**Nothing is removed from the record.** The `.jsonl` files are byte-for-byte
as Claude Code wrote them, images included, and they are the authoritative
submission; only the derived readable view substitutes the placeholder. The
images are course handout pages, not private data. `sessions/` is about 62 MB,
most of it the `.jsonl` files.

"""
A small multilayer perceptron in numpy, for Assignment 2.

You should not need to open this file. `kestrel.py` wraps everything the
assignment asks for. It is here so that nothing in the pipeline is a black box
you could not inspect if you wanted to.

    MLP(sizes)              e.g. MLP([160, 64, 1]) -- one hidden layer of 64
    .fit(X, Y, ...)         Adam, mini-batch, optional early stopping
    .predict(X)
    .hidden(X, layer=1)     the activations of a hidden layer -- the learned
                            representation, which is what gets frozen and reused
    .copy_body_from(other)  copy all layers except the last, which is how a
                            fine-tuned network is initialised from an encoder

Everything is float64 numpy. No GPU, no autograd; the backward pass is written
out. You are not responsible for it. You ARE responsible for knowing what the
model consumes, produces, and assumes.
"""
import numpy as np


def _relu(z):
    return np.maximum(z, 0.0)


class MLP:
    def __init__(self, sizes, seed=0):
        """sizes = [n_in, n_hidden_1, ..., n_out]."""
        self.sizes = list(sizes)
        rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        self.W, self.b = [], []
        for a, b in zip(self.sizes[:-1], self.sizes[1:]):
            # He initialisation
            self.W.append(rng.normal(0, np.sqrt(2.0 / a), (a, b)))
            self.b.append(np.zeros(b))

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------ core
    def _forward(self, X):
        acts = [X]
        h = X
        for i, (W, b) in enumerate(zip(self.W, self.b)):
            z = h @ W + b
            h = z if i == len(self.W) - 1 else _relu(z)   # linear output layer
            acts.append(h)
        return acts

    def predict(self, X):
        return self._forward(np.asarray(X, dtype=float))[-1]

    def hidden(self, X, layer=1):
        """Activations after `layer` hidden layers.  layer=1 is the first.

        This is the learned representation. Handout 9 S3.4 is about which layer
        to take; Assignment 2 fixes it at the first so that every submission's
        table is comparable.
        """
        return self._forward(np.asarray(X, dtype=float))[layer]

    def copy_body_from(self, other):
        """Copy every layer except the last.  Shapes must match.

        This is what turns a pre-trained encoder into the starting point for a
        fine-tuned predictor: the body carries over, the output layer is new.
        """
        n = len(self.W) - 1
        for i in range(n):
            self.W[i] = other.W[i].copy()
            self.b[i] = other.b[i].copy()
        return self

    # ------------------------------------------------------------------- fit
    def fit(self, X, Y, epochs=200, batch_size=64, lr=1e-3, seed=0,
            X_val=None, Y_val=None, patience=None, verbose=False):
        """Mini-batch Adam on mean squared error.

        If X_val/Y_val and `patience` are given, stops when validation MSE has
        not improved for `patience` epochs and restores the best weights.
        Returns a history dict.
        """
        X = np.asarray(X, dtype=float)
        Y = np.asarray(Y, dtype=float)
        if Y.ndim == 1:
            Y = Y[:, None]
        rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
        n = len(X)

        mW = [np.zeros_like(w) for w in self.W]
        vW = [np.zeros_like(w) for w in self.W]
        mb = [np.zeros_like(b) for b in self.b]
        vb = [np.zeros_like(b) for b in self.b]
        b1, b2, eps, step = 0.9, 0.999, 1e-8, 0

        hist = {"train": [], "val": []}
        best, best_epoch, best_w = np.inf, 0, None

        for ep in range(epochs):
            order = rng.permutation(n)
            for s in range(0, n, batch_size):
                idx = order[s:s + batch_size]
                xb, yb = X[idx], Y[idx]
                acts = self._forward(xb)
                delta = 2.0 * (acts[-1] - yb) / len(idx)
                step += 1
                for i in range(len(self.W) - 1, -1, -1):
                    gW = acts[i].T @ delta
                    gb = delta.sum(axis=0)
                    if i > 0:
                        delta = (delta @ self.W[i].T) * (acts[i] > 0)
                    for g, m, v, p in ((gW, mW, vW, self.W), (gb, mb, vb, self.b)):
                        m[i] = b1 * m[i] + (1 - b1) * g
                        v[i] = b2 * v[i] + (1 - b2) * g * g
                        mh = m[i] / (1 - b1 ** step)
                        vh = v[i] / (1 - b2 ** step)
                        p[i] -= lr * mh / (np.sqrt(vh) + eps)

            tr = float(np.mean((self.predict(X) - Y) ** 2))
            hist["train"].append(tr)
            if X_val is not None:
                Yv = np.asarray(Y_val, dtype=float)
                if Yv.ndim == 1:
                    Yv = Yv[:, None]
                va = float(np.mean((self.predict(X_val) - Yv) ** 2))
                hist["val"].append(va)
                if va < best - 1e-9:
                    best, best_epoch = va, ep
                    best_w = ([w.copy() for w in self.W], [b.copy() for b in self.b])
                elif patience is not None and ep - best_epoch >= patience:
                    if verbose:
                        print(f"early stop at epoch {ep}, best {best:.4f} @ {best_epoch}")
                    break
            if verbose and ep % 20 == 0:
                print(f"epoch {ep:4d}  train {tr:10.4f}"
                      + (f"  val {hist['val'][-1]:10.4f}" if hist["val"] else ""))

        if patience is not None and best_w is not None:
            self.W, self.b = best_w
        hist["best_epoch"] = best_epoch
        return hist

- **.gitignore**. A1 was under git so you could sync between your Windows and Mac machines. Do you want this folder under git too?

## Q1: Where do the n = 50 panels come from?

**Not from the 1,000 dev panels.** They come from the **2,000 train panels**. Each file has one job:

| File | Rows | Role |
|---|---|---|
| `labeled_train.csv` | 2,000 | The only source of labels to **fit** on. n = 50 means 50 of these. |
| `labeled_dev.csv` | 1,000 | **Never trained on.** Every model is scored on all 1,000. |
| `labeled_test.csv` | 1,000 | Scored once, at the very end. |
| `unlabeled_traces.csv.gz` | 20,000 | Gauges only, no strength. Used only for pre-training. |

If you trained on dev rows and then scored on dev, the score would be contaminated. Dev works as a fair yardstick only because the model has never seen it.

## Q2: What are pre-training and the encoder?

### The problem pre-training solves

Each panel has 160 gauge readings. The data dictionary says these are **redundant**: they are 160 views of a few underlying conditions (how hot the part got, how fast it heated, how well the resin flowed, how much contamination there was). Two thermocouples in the same oven zone say almost the same thing.

With only 50 labelled panels, learning from 160 raw numbers is hard. It would help to first compress each panel into a smaller, more meaningful description. You'd want the description to capture something like "this panel ran hot and resin-starved" instead of listing 160 raw readings.

The key point: **learning that description needs no strength labels.** It only needs to learn how the gauges relate to each other, and there are 20,000 free traces for that.

### Pre-training: a fill-in-the-blanks game

Pre-training builds this network ([kestrel.py:132-151](starter/kestrel.py#L132-L151)):

```
 160 gauges ──► 64 ──► 16 ──► 160 gauges
 (30% blanked)   │                (all of them, the originals)
                 └─ this layer = "the representation"
```

The training loop, using the 20,000 unlabelled traces:
1. Take a panel's 160 gauges and blank out a random 30% of them (set to 0, which is the average reading after standardising).
2. Feed the damaged version in, and ask the network to output **all 160 original values**.
3. Score it on how well it rebuilt the readings (squared error), and adjust the weights.
4. Repeat for 40 passes over the data, blanking a **different** random 30% each time. That way it can't memorise one pattern of gaps.

The "label" here is the data itself, which is why this is called **self-supervised**. Strength is never used.

**Why this teaches the network anything useful.** To guess a blanked thermocouple, it has to work out from the other gauges what the oven was doing. To do that across many panels, it has to learn the underlying conditions. The squeeze through 64 and then 16 numbers makes this worse for it: it cannot copy 160 values through, so it has to compress.

### The encoder

After pre-training, keep the first part (**160 → 64**) and discard the rest (64 → 16 → 160), which only existed to make the game possible. The part you keep is the **encoder**. For any panel it turns 160 gauges into **64 numbers**, and those 64 numbers are the **representation** (`representation()` at [kestrel.py:165](starter/kestrel.py#L165)).

The bet is that these 64 numbers describe the panel's process conditions better than the 160 raw gauges, so a small number of labels goes further.

Training three encoders with seeds 0, 1, 2 gives three somewhat different encoders: same game, different random starts and blanking patterns. That's the second source of randomness from before.

## Q3: Which steps use labelled vs unlabelled data?

| Method | 20k unlabelled? | n labelled? | What gets learned from the n labels |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1. Ridge on raw gauges | no | yes | 160 linear weights on the gauges |
| 2. Frozen encoder + ridge | yes (encoder, once) | yes | Only ridge weights on the 64 features. The encoder is **frozen**, so its weights don't change. |
| 3. Frozen **random** encoder + ridge | no | yes | Same as 2, but the encoder **never played the game**. Its weights are random. |
| 4. Network from scratch | no | yes | A whole 160 → 64 → 1 network, starting from random weights |
| 5. Fine-tuned | yes (starting point) | yes | The same 160 → 64 → 1 network, but its 160 → 64 layer **starts** from the pre-trained encoder, then all weights keep training on the labels at a smaller learning rate |

A few things to notice:
- **Methods 4 and 5 have the same shape**, and the 160 → 64 layer matches the encoder. That's what allows the transplant: `copy_body_from` copies every layer except the output layer. So 4 vs 5 asks whether starting from pre-trained weights beats starting from random ones.
- **Method 3 is the control.** A random 160 → 64 layer with a ReLU still produces 64 nonlinear features, and those might help ridge on their own. Without row 3, if row 2 beats row 1 you couldn't tell whether pre-training learned something or the architecture alone helped (Handout 9 §3.3). Row 2 vs row 3 isolates what the fill-in-the-blanks game added.
- **Frozen vs fine-tuned.** Freezing learns very few things from the labels (65 ridge coefficients), which is safe when labels are scarce. Fine-tuning lets the encoder adjust toward predicting strength, which is more flexible but has more weights to fit from few labels. The brief's rule of thumb (freeze at tens of labels, fine-tune at hundreds to thousands, train from scratch at tens of thousands) is about this trade-off.

Want to check your understanding before we run anything? One question to try: **why might ridge on the raw gauges stay stuck even at n = 1,000, while a network could do better?** Re-read the "two failure modes multiply rather than add" line in the data dictionary first.

## The numbers: 2,000, 1,000 and 50

Each of these numbers means something different:

| Number | What it is |
|---|---|
| **2,000** | All the labelled panels Kestrel actually has, in `labeled_train.csv`. In the story, this is the five years of destructive tests. |
| **50, 100, 250, 1,000** | The **label counts n**. Each is a pretend budget: "what if Kestrel had tested only n panels?" Each is a random subset of the 2,000. |
| **1,000 (dev)** | A separate file of 1,000 extra tested panels, used only to **score** models. |
| **1,000 (test)** | Another 1,000 panels, scored once at the end. |

So "1,000" shows up twice by coincidence. The largest label count is n = 1,000, and the dev file also happens to have 1,000 rows. They are unrelated: a model trained on n = 1,000 train panels is scored on the 1,000 dev panels.

The files contain 4,000 labelled panels in total. Only the 2,000 in train count as Kestrel's labels. Dev and test exist so we can grade models fairly, on panels they never saw.

The table stops at n = 1,000, but Kestrel has 2,000. Keep that in mind for the memo's question about the method to deploy at Kestrel's current label count.

## Your answer about the incumbent

Part of it is on the right track, and part of it is the exact trap the rubric names. Here is why.

**"1,000 is not enough data for a linear model."** For a linear model, 1,000 rows is a lot. Ridge fits 161 numbers (160 weights plus an intercept), so that's about 6 rows per coefficient, and ridge's penalty handles the rest.

Shortage is a real issue at n = 50, where there are fewer rows than coefficients. At 1,000 it's much less believable. The rubric warns against this diagnosis directly: *"Diagnosing the incumbent as short of data."*

**"Collinearity."** The gauges are highly collinear, but ridge is built for exactly that. The penalty spreads weight across redundant gauges instead of letting the fit blow up. Collinearity makes the individual weights hard to interpret. It doesn't make the predictions bad.

**"Non-linear."** This is the promising part. Look at what the data dictionary says about the physics:
- **The failure modes multiply.** Weak resin flow and weak cure combine like "flow × cure." A surplus in one can't make up for a deficit in the other.
- **Contamination has a threshold.** Below it, nothing happens. Above it, strength falls sharply.

A linear model can only produce *weighted sums*. Every gauge pushes strength up or down by a fixed amount, regardless of the other gauges. So it can't express "high cure helps only if flow is also high," or "contamination matters only past a threshold."

## Why this matters: two kinds of limit

This is the bias–variance distinction from Lecture 3:

| | Data shortage (variance) | Wrong model shape (bias) |
|---|---|---|
| Cause | Too few rows to pin down the weights | The model *can't express* the true relationship |
| What more data does | Error keeps falling | Error **plateaus**. Even with the perfect weights, a weighted sum is still the wrong shape. |
| Fix | More tests | A different model or features, not more tests |

The engineer is betting on the left column ("another 2,000 tests and re-fit"). If the right column is the true story, his $8.8M buys almost nothing.

That's the diagnosis to settle from the table, not to assert in advance. When it's built, three comparisons will tell you which column applies:
1. **Ridge at n = 50 vs n = 1,000.** Does the error keep dropping, or flatten out?
2. **Ridge vs the do-nothing baseline** (predict the mean strength). How much of the variation does ridge explain at all?
3. **Ridge vs a network at the same n.** If a network does clearly better on the *same* panels, the information is in the gauges and the linear shape can't use it. That points to bias, not shortage.

Before we run anything, write your expectations down in a sentence or two. For example: "I expect ridge to improve only slightly between 50 and 1,000 and to stall well above zero, because…". That's the course's "write it down first" step, and it gives you something to be surprised by.

## Next step

The deadline is Thursday and nothing has been run yet. Once you've written your expectations, these are the decisions I need from you to build the table:
1. **Seed for the two frozen rows' ridge.** `seed=replicate`, to match the other rows, is the natural choice.
2. **Git or not** for this folder.

Then I'll write `analysis/` (pre-train 3 encoders once, then the two nested loops, all scored on dev) and we'll go through the table together.

I logged the 2,000/1,000/50 clarification and the challenge to your incumbent answer in [NOTES.md](NOTES.md).

Your picture of the frozen row is right. The "draws" are not a step after that: they decide **which** 50 (or 100, …) panels you fit on in the first place.

## What a draw is

Kestrel has 2,000 labelled panels. At n = 50 there are many ways to pick 50 of them, and the result depends on which 50 you pick. So we pick **5 different sets of 50**. Each set is one **draw**, numbered r = 0, 1, 2, 3, 4.

```
2,000 train panels
   ├── draw 0: panels #17, #402, #1288, ... (50 of them)
   ├── draw 1: a different 50
   ├── draw 2: a different 50
   ├── draw 3: a different 50
   └── draw 4: a different 50
```

`label_subset(50, r)` returns those 50 row numbers. The same happens at 100, 250 and 1,000: five different random subsets at each size.

The key rule: **within a draw, all five methods train on exactly the same panels.** Any difference between methods inside a draw is then down to the method, not to luck in which panels they saw.

## One pass of the loop: n = 50, draw 0

1. Get the 50 panels: their gauges (50 × 160) and their strengths (50 numbers).
2. Fit each method on those 50 and score it on all 1,000 dev panels:

| Method | What happens with the 50 panels | Fits |
|---|---|---|
| Raw ridge | Ridge maps the 160 gauges to strength | 1 |
| Frozen pre-trained + ridge | Pass the 50 panels through **encoder 0**'s first hidden layer to get 64 numbers each, fit ridge on those, and score. Repeat with **encoder 1** and **encoder 2**. | **3** |
| Frozen random + ridge | Same as above, but through the never-trained encoder | 1 |
| From scratch | Train a 160 → 64 → 1 network from random weights (37 to train, 13 to decide when to stop) | 1 |
| Fine-tuned | Same network, but its first layer starts as a copy of encoder r mod 3, here encoder 0 | 1 |

That's **7 dev scores** for this draw.

3. Move on to draw 1, which is a new set of 50 panels, and repeat. Fine-tuning now starts from encoder 1, draw 2 from encoder 2, draw 3 from encoder 0 again, and so on.

## Putting the cell together

After 5 draws at n = 50, each method's cell holds:

| Method | Scores in the cell |
|---|---|
| Raw ridge | 5 (one per draw) |
| Frozen pre-trained | **15** (5 draws × 3 encoders) |
| Frozen random | 5 |
| From scratch | 5 |
| Fine-tuned | 5 (encoders used: 0, 1, 2, 0, 1) |

The table cell is the **mean ± SD** of those scores. Then the whole thing repeats for n = 100, 250 and 1,000.

As code, the whole table is:

```
encoders = [pretrain(traces, seed=s) for s in 0, 1, 2]   # once, before the loops
rand_enc = random_encoder()

for n in 50, 100, 250, 1000:
    for r in 0..4:                       # the 5 draws
        idx = label_subset(n, r)         # which n panels
        X, y = train gauges[idx], train strength[idx]
        fit all five methods on (X, y), score each on dev
```

## What the SD in each cell means

Each SD measures how much the result moves when you change things that **shouldn't matter**:
- **Which panels happened to get tested** (the draw), for every row.
- **Which pre-training run you got** (the encoder), for the frozen row, and partly for the fine-tuned row.

If two methods' means differ by less than that spread, the table can't tell them apart. That's why the brief insists on the draws.

Does that clear it up? If so, have a go at [expectations.md](expectations.md), and after that I'll write `analysis/`.

It's the error you'd get by **ignoring the gauges completely**.

## Where it comes from

1. The average strength of the 2,000 train panels is **32.8 MPa**.
2. Use that as the "prediction" for every one of the 1,000 dev panels: "every panel is 32.8 MPa."
3. For each dev panel, take the miss (actual minus 32.8), square it, and average over all 1,000.

That average squared miss is **188.9 MPa²**. It's the **MSE** (mean squared error), the same score every model in the table gets.

## How to read it

- **The units are squared** (MPa²), which makes the number hard to picture. Its square root, **13.7 MPa**, is the typical miss. Strength is about 32.8 ± 13.7 MPa, so guessing the average is off by around 14 MPa on a typical panel.
- **It's the variance of strength on dev.** Predicting the mean leaves all of the panel-to-panel variation unexplained, so the MSE equals the variance (188.8). The extra 0.1 is because the train mean differs very slightly from the dev mean.

## Why it matters

It's the floor for "learned nothing." Any model that uses the gauges should beat it:
- **Near 188.9**: the model barely used the gauges.
- **Halfway to 0, around 94**: the model explained about half the variation in strength (R² ≈ 0.5).
- **Near 0**: almost perfect.

For any model, **1 − MSE / 188.9** is the share of strength variation it explains. That's often the easiest way to say "how good" to someone who isn't a modeller.

The brief's Question 1 asks you to compare the incumbent against this number explicitly. So now, **Question 1**: where do you think raw ridge lands at n = 50 and at n = 1,000 relative to 188.9, and does it keep falling or flatten as n grows, and why?

Your reasoning is sound, and it's the key point of Question 1. Three refinements:

**(a) n = 50, "near 188.9."** Reasonable, but think about *why* it can't go much past it. Ridge with 160 gauges and 50 panels has more coefficients than rows. The penalty handles that by shrinking all the weights toward zero, and a ridge with weights near zero just predicts the mean. So the penalty works like a safety net: ridge tends to fall back toward 188.9 instead of doing much worse.

The catch is that it picks the penalty strength on only 13 held-out panels. That choice is noisy, so expect a **large SD** at n = 50. Some draws could even land above 188.9.

**(b) and (c) "a floor it can't go under because the model is the wrong shape."** That's the bias explanation, and it's the right hypothesis. But a flattening curve **on its own doesn't prove it**. A curve also flattens when it hits **irreducible noise**, the part of strength the gauges can't predict at all (the noise-floor idea from A1). Both stories look the same in one row of the table:

| Why ridge flattens | Can a different model at the same n do better? |
|---|---|
| Wrong shape (bias) | **Yes.** A model that can bend uses information ridge can't. |
| Noise floor | **No.** No model can, because the information isn't in the gauges. |

So the evidence that settles it is not ridge's own curve. It's **ridge against the networks at n = 1,000**, on the same panels. The rubric asks how "the table tells the two apart," and this is the answer to look for when the table is in.

**One sharpening, optional.** If you want, say *where* you expect it to flatten. The gauges are redundant views of a few underlying conditions, so the linear part might be learned with fairly few panels. That could mean an early flattening, not a gradual one. Either guess is fine; the point is to commit to something you can check.

I'll put your answer into [expectations.md](expectations.md) with these notes when we finish all eight.

### Question 2 of 8: Frozen pre-trained encoder + ridge

Each panel's 160 gauges go through a pre-trained encoder's first hidden layer, which outputs 64 numbers. Ridge is fit on those 64 numbers. The encoder learned only from the 20,000 unlabelled traces, by filling in blanked-out gauges. It never saw a strength value.

Things to think about:
- What does the encoder's training game force it to learn about the gauges?
- Ridge is still linear, but now it's linear in *what*?
- How many coefficients does ridge have to learn here, compared with before?

ASSISTANT  [2026-11-01T20:24:26.329Z]
